passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a new dietary supplement on exercise performance in healthy adults. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 120 participants aged 18–35. Participants were randomly assigned to either the supplement group (n=60) or placebo group (n=60). Over 8 weeks, all participants performed a standardized treadmill test at baseline and after the intervention. The primary outcome was peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak). Table 1 summarizes the mean baseline and post-intervention VO2peak values, the mean change, and the post-intervention standard deviation for each group. In addition, secondary outcomes included time to exhaustion and perceived exertion scores. The supplement group showed a mean increase of 3.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in VO2peak compared to 1.1 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in the placebo group. Statistical analysis revealed a p-value of 0.004 for the between-group difference. No adverse events were reported. The authors concluded that the supplement may enhance aerobic capacity in young adults.
table_data:
Table 1. VO2peak by group (mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹)

| Group | Baseline | Post-intervention | Mean change | Post SD |
|-------|----------|-------------------|-------------|---------|
| Placebo | 41.4 | 42.5 | 1.1 | 4.3 |
| Supplement | 42.5 | 45.7 | 3.2 | 3.9 |
stem: According to Table 1, what was the mean VO2peak for the supplement group after the intervention?
explanation: Table 1 lists the post-intervention mean VO2peak for the supplement group as 45.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.
trap: Option C (3.2) is the mean increase, not the absolute post-intervention value.

stem: If the supplement group had a mean VO2peak of 45.7 with SD 3.9, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean, assuming n=60?
trap: Underestimating the margin and choosing a narrow interval such as 45.00–46.40; the margin is 1.96 × 3.9/√60 ≈ 0.99 on each side of 45.7.
